pagetitle: "Group theory"

# Group theory {#sec-group-theory}

Groups are the algebra of symmetry. Whenever a set of transformations can be composed, undone and contains the
transformation that does nothing, it forms a group, and much of what can be said about a symmetric object follows
from the multiplication table of its group alone. This chapter has four sections. Groups defines groups, abelian
groups, orders, subgroups, generated subgroups and normal subgroups, with the integers modulo $n$, the permutation
group $S_3$ and the rotation groups as running examples. Cosets and quotient groups slices a group into the cosets of
a subgroup, proves Lagrange's theorem, turns the cosets of a normal subgroup into a group, and introduces group
actions with their orbits and stabilisers. Homomorphisms studies the maps that respect multiplication, their kernels,
isomorphisms, the first isomorphism theorem and conjugation. Representations and Schur's lemma lets a group act by
matrices, splits representations into irreducible pieces and proves Schur's lemma on the maps that commute with an
irreducible representation. Every statement is followed by three examples and three exercises with hidden solutions,
and many of the computations are carried out with Sage's group theory modules.

## Groups {#sec-groups}

Symmetry is the organising principle of much of mathematics and physics: the isometries of a space form a group, the
transformations that leave the equations of a field theory unchanged form a group, and conserved quantities come from
these groups. This section defines groups and subgroups and works every notion on small finite groups and on the
rotation groups, so that the Lie groups of @sec-lie-groups and the coset spaces of @sec-coset-spaces arrive with
their algebra already familiar.

### Groups

The transformations of an object that preserve its shape can be performed one after the other, undone, and include
the transformation that leaves everything in place. The definition below keeps only these three properties and
forgets what is being transformed.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-group}
#### Group

A **group** is a set $G$ with a multiplication $(g, h) \mapsto gh$ that is associative, $(gh)k = g(hk)$, has an
**identity** $e$ with $eg = ge = g$, and has an **inverse** $g^{-1}$ for every $g$ with $gg^{-1} = g^{-1}g = e$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The first example is arithmetic on a clock face. Adding hours modulo $n$ is associative, has $0$ as identity, and
every hour can be undone by going forward the remaining hours, so the residues modulo $n$ form a group.

::: {#exm-group-zn}
#### Integers modulo $n$

$\mathbb{Z}_n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ with addition modulo $n$ (@exm-quotient-zn) is a group: the identity is $0$
and the inverse of $k$ is $n - k$. The rotations of a regular hexagon by multiples of $60^\circ$ form a group with
the same multiplication table as $\mathbb{Z}_6$ (@fig-cayley-graph).
:::

The second example has a multiplication that is composition of maps. Composition of functions is always
associative, so bijections of a finite set form a group as soon as the identity map and inverse maps are included.

::: {#exm-group-s3}
#### Permutations

The bijections of $\{1, 2, 3\}$ to itself (@exm-bijection-finite) form the **symmetric group** $S_3$ under
composition, with the identity map as identity and the inverse map as inverse; the rotations and reflections of
a triangle form a group with the same table (@exr-s3-table). In general the permutations of $n$ objects form
$S_n$.
:::

The third example brings in infinite groups, which are the ones met most often in geometry. Matrices compose by
matrix multiplication, which is associative, and the invertible ones have inverses by definition.

::: {#exm-group-matrix}
#### Matrix groups

The invertible $n \times n$ real matrices form the **general linear group** $GL(n, \mathbb{R})$ under matrix
multiplication; the identity is the unit matrix and the inverse the matrix inverse. The rotations of the plane,
$R(\alpha) = \begin{pmatrix} \cos\alpha & -\sin\alpha \\ \sin\alpha & \cos\alpha \end{pmatrix}$, form $SO(2)$ with
$R(\alpha)R(\beta) = R(\alpha + \beta)$; the rotations of space form $SO(3)$; the matrices @eq-su2-matrix form
$SU(2)$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Deciding whether a set with an operation is a group means checking each axiom, and the failures are as instructive
as the successes. The first exercise tests four candidates, some of which miss one axiom only.

::: {#exr-group-axioms}
#### Checking the axioms

Decide whether the following are groups: the non-zero real numbers under multiplication; the integers under
subtraction; the $2 \times 2$ real matrices under matrix multiplication; the rotations and reflections of the
plane that fix the origin.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Non-zero reals under multiplication: yes, abelian. Integers under subtraction: no, since $(a - b) - c \neq a -
(b - c)$ and there is no identity ($a - e = a$ gives $e = 0$ but $0 - a \neq a$). All $2 \times 2$ matrices: no,
the zero matrix has no inverse; the invertible ones form $GL(2, \mathbb{R})$. Rotations and reflections fixing
the origin: yes, the orthogonal group $O(2)$, non-abelian, with $SO(2)$ as a normal subgroup of index $2$.
:::

Multiplication modulo $n$ is associative and has the identity $1$, so the only question for the non-zero residues is
whether every element has an inverse. The second exercise shows that the answer depends on whether $n$ is prime.

::: {#exr-grp-units-mod5}
#### Multiplication modulo $5$ and modulo $6$

Show that $\{1, 2, 3, 4\}$ is a group under multiplication modulo $5$ by writing its multiplication table and finding
every inverse. Explain why $\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5\}$ is not a group under multiplication modulo $6$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Modulo $5$ the product of two non-zero residues is non-zero ($5$ is prime), so the set is closed; the inverses are
$1^{-1} = 1$, $2^{-1} = 3$, $3^{-1} = 2$, $4^{-1} = 4$, read off the table as the column containing $1$. Modulo $6$ the
set is not closed, $2 \cdot 3 = 0$, and $2, 3, 4$ have no inverse; only $\{1, 5\}$, the residues coprime to $6$, form a
group. With Sage's `Zmod`:

{{< sage exr-grp-units-mod5 >}}
:::

The axioms ask for an identity and for inverses but do not say that these are unique. The third exercise derives
uniqueness from the axioms, together with the rule for inverting a product that is used throughout the chapter.

::: {#exr-grp-uniqueness}
#### Uniqueness of the identity and of inverses

Show from the axioms that a group has only one identity, that each element has only one inverse, and that $(gh)^{-1}
= h^{-1}g^{-1}$. Deduce that the equation $gx = k$ has exactly one solution $x$ for given $g, k$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
If $e$ and $e'$ are identities then $e = ee' = e'$. If $h$ and $h'$ are inverses of $g$ then $h = he = h(gh') = (hg)h'
= eh' = h'$. Since $(gh)(h^{-1}g^{-1}) = g(hh^{-1})g^{-1} = gg^{-1} = e$, and similarly in the other order,
$h^{-1}g^{-1}$ is the inverse of $gh$: the order is reversed, as for putting on and taking off socks and shoes.
Finally $x = g^{-1}k$ solves $gx = k$, and any solution satisfies $x = g^{-1}(gx) = g^{-1}k$. So every row of a
multiplication table contains each element exactly once.
:::
::::

In a group the order of the factors can matter, as the matrix examples already suggest. Groups in which it never
matters are singled out by the next definition.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-abelian-group}
#### Abelian group

A group is **abelian** (or **commutative**) if $gh = hg$ for all $g, h \in G$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The groups built from addition of numbers or of angles are abelian, because addition commutes. The example also
identifies the rotations of the plane with the unit complex numbers, two descriptions of one abelian group.

::: {#exm-abelian-zn}
#### $\mathbb{Z}_n$, $SO(2)$ and $U(1)$

$\mathbb{Z}_n$ is abelian, since addition commutes; so is $SO(2)$, since $R(\alpha)R(\beta) = R(\alpha + \beta) =
R(\beta)R(\alpha)$, and the unit complex numbers $U(1) = \{e^{i\alpha}\}$ under multiplication, which
$e^{i\alpha} \mapsto R(\alpha)$ identifies with $SO(2)$. $U(1)$ is the gauge group of electromagnetism and of
Part III.
:::

Permutations of three objects already fail to commute. Composing two transpositions in the two possible orders gives
the two different three-cycles, which is the smallest instance of a non-abelian group.

::: {#exm-nonabelian-s3}
#### $S_3$ is not abelian

$(1\,2)(1\,3) \neq (1\,3)(1\,2)$: one composition is the cycle $(1\,2\,3)$ and the other $(1\,3\,2)$
(@prp-s3-facts, @exr-s3-table). $S_3$ is the smallest non-abelian group, and @fig-cayley-graph shows its
Cayley graph next to that of $\mathbb{Z}_6$.
:::

Rotations of space behave like permutations rather than like rotations of the plane. Two quarter turns about
different axes, applied in the two orders, leave an object in different positions.

::: {#exm-nonabelian-so3}
#### $SO(3)$ is not abelian

A rotation by $90^\circ$ about the $X$-axis followed by one about the $Z$-axis differs from the reverse order,
as turning a book shows; $SU(2)$ is not abelian either. Non-abelian gauge groups are the subject of Part IV.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
![Cayley graphs drawn with Sage's group and graph modules: vertices are group elements and an edge from $g$ to
$gs$ is drawn for each generator $s$. Left: $\mathbb{Z}_6$ with generator $1$, a single cycle. Right: $S_3$ with
generators $(1\,2)$ (red) and $(1\,2\,3)$ (blue), two triangles joined by three edges. Generated by
`figures/cayley_graph.sage`.](figures/cayley_graph.svg){#fig-cayley-graph width=85%}

{{< interactive cayley_graph 460 >}}

The interactive version shows the full multiplication table of $S_3$: the cell in row $g$ and column $h$ holds the
product $gh$ (first $h$, then $g$), and hovering a cell displays it. The rows and columns list the three-cycles before
the transpositions, and the colours, blue for even and orange for odd products, split the table into four blocks.

Commutativity can be tested pair by pair, and for a non-abelian group it is natural to ask how many pairs still
commute. The first exercise does this count with Sage for five groups of orders $4$, $6$ and $8$.

::: {#exr-grp-abelian-test}
#### Counting commuting pairs

For $\mathbb{Z}_6$, $\mathbb{Z}_2 \times \mathbb{Z}_2$, $S_3$, the symmetry group $D_4$ of a square and the quaternion
group $Q_8 = \{\pm 1, \pm i, \pm j, \pm k\}$, decide which are abelian and count the ordered pairs $(g, h)$ with $gh =
hg$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\mathbb{Z}_6$ and $\mathbb{Z}_2 \times \mathbb{Z}_2$ are abelian, so all $36$ and $16$ pairs commute. In $S_3$ the
number of commuting pairs is the sum over $g$ of the number of elements commuting with $g$: the identity commutes with
all $6$, each transposition only with $e$ and itself, each three-cycle with $e$ and the two three-cycles, so the count
is $6 + 3 \cdot 2 + 2 \cdot 3 = 18$ of $36$. $D_4$ and $Q_8$
both give $40$ of $64$, although they are different groups:

{{< sage exr-grp-abelian-test >}}
:::

A simple condition on the elements can force a group to be abelian. The second exercise asks for the short
computation that shows this when every element is its own inverse.

::: {#exr-grp-square-identity}
#### Groups of exponent two

Show that if $g^2 = e$ for every element $g$ of a group, the group is abelian. Give an example of order $4$ and check
that $S_3$ does not satisfy the hypothesis.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Each element is its own inverse, $g^{-1} = g$. Then $gh = (gh)^{-1} = h^{-1}g^{-1} = hg$, using @exr-grp-uniqueness for
the inverse of a product. The group $\mathbb{Z}_2 \times \mathbb{Z}_2 = \{(0,0), (1,0), (0,1), (1,1)\}$ with
componentwise addition modulo $2$ is an example of order $4$. In $S_3$ the three-cycle $(1\,2\,3)$ has
$(1\,2\,3)^2 = (1\,3\,2) \neq e$, so the hypothesis fails, as it must since $S_3$ is not abelian.
:::

The failure of commutativity is measured by the commutator $ghg^{-1}h^{-1}$, which equals $e$ exactly when $g$ and $h$
commute. The third exercise computes it in a group of triangular matrices that contains an abelian subgroup.

::: {#exr-grp-commutator}
#### Commutators of triangular matrices

Show that the upper triangular matrices $\begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ 0 & d \end{pmatrix}$ with $ad \neq 0$ form a group
under matrix multiplication, compute the commutator of $g = \begin{pmatrix} a & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ and $h =
\begin{pmatrix} 1 & b \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$, and show that the matrices with $a = d = 1$ multiply by adding the
entries $b$, so that they form an abelian group.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The product of two upper triangular matrices is upper triangular with diagonal entries multiplied, $\begin{pmatrix} a
& b \\ 0 & d \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} a' & b' \\ 0 & d' \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} aa' & ab' + bd' \\ 0 &
dd' \end{pmatrix}$, and the inverse $\begin{pmatrix} 1/a & -b/(ad) \\ 0 & 1/d \end{pmatrix}$ is again upper
triangular. Then $ghg^{-1}h^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & ab \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -b \\ 0 & 1
\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & (a - 1)b \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$, which is the identity only if $a = 1$ or $b = 0$:
the group is not abelian. For $a = d = 1$ the product formula gives the entry $b + b'$, so these matrices multiply as
the real numbers add, and they commute.
:::
::::

Repeating a single element of a finite group must eventually return to the identity, because there are only finitely
many powers. The next definition measures how long that takes, and how large the group is.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-order}
#### Order

The **order** $|G|$ of a group is its number of elements (possibly infinite). The **order of an element** $g$ is
the least $n > 0$ with $g^n = e$, or infinite if there is none.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The symmetric group is small enough to list completely, and its elements fall into three kinds by their order. The
example reads the orders off the cycle structure of each permutation.

::: {#exm-order-s3}
#### Orders in $S_3$

$|S_3| = 6$ (@prp-s3-facts); the identity has order $1$, the three transpositions $(1\,2), (1\,3), (2\,3)$ have
order $2$ and the two three-cycles have order $3$ (@exr-s3-table). Every order divides $6$, as Lagrange's
theorem of @sec-cosets-quotients explains.
:::

In $\mathbb{Z}_6$ the $n$-th power of an element $k$ is the sum $nk$, so the order of $k$ is the least $n$ with $nk$
divisible by $6$. The example lists these orders and finds an element whose order is the order of the group.

::: {#exm-order-zn}
#### Orders in $\mathbb{Z}_6$

$|\mathbb{Z}_6| = 6$; the element $1$ has order $6$, $2$ and $4$ have order $3$, $3$ has order $2$ and $0$ has
order $1$. The element $1$ generates the whole group, which is what makes $\mathbb{Z}_6$ **cyclic**.
:::

In an infinite group the order of an element can be finite or infinite. Rotations of the plane show both
possibilities, depending on whether the angle is a rational multiple of a full turn.

::: {#exm-order-infinite}
#### Infinite groups

$SO(2)$, $SO(3)$, $SU(2)$ and $(\mathbb{Z}, +)$ have infinite order; in $SO(2)$ the rotation by $2\pi/n$ has order
$n$ and the rotation by an irrational multiple of $\pi$ has infinite order. In $SU(2)$ the element $-1$ has
order $2$ and $e^{tT_3}$ has order $4\pi/t$ when that is an integer (@sec-exponential).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The orders of the elements of a cyclic group follow a simple pattern governed by greatest common divisors. The first
exercise computes them for $\mathbb{Z}_{12}$ and counts how many elements have each order.

::: {#exr-grp-orders-z12}
#### Orders in $\mathbb{Z}_{12}$

Find the order of every element of $\mathbb{Z}_{12}$, count the elements of each order, and check that the order of
$k$ is $12/\gcd(k, 12)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The order of $k$ is the least $n > 0$ with $12 \mid nk$, which is $12/\gcd(k, 12)$. There is one element of order
$1$ ($0$), one of order $2$ ($6$), two of order $3$ ($4, 8$), two of order $4$ ($3, 9$), two of order $6$ ($2, 10$) and
four of order $12$ ($1, 5, 7, 11$); the number of elements of order $d$ is Euler's $\varphi(d)$, the number of residues
coprime to $d$:

{{< sage exr-grp-orders-z12 >}}
:::

Inverting or conjugating an element should not change how long its powers take to return to the identity. The
second exercise proves this and uses it to compare the orders of $gh$ and $hg$.

::: {#exr-grp-order-inverse}
#### Orders of inverses and conjugates

Show that $g$, $g^{-1}$ and $kgk^{-1}$ have the same order for all $g, k$, and deduce that $gh$ and $hg$ have the same
order. Check the last statement on $g = (1\,2)$, $h = (1\,3)$ in $S_3$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$(g^{-1})^n = (g^n)^{-1}$ is $e$ exactly when $g^n = e$. For the conjugate, $(kgk^{-1})^n = kg^nk^{-1}$ because the inner
factors $k^{-1}k$ cancel, and $kg^nk^{-1} = e$ exactly when $g^n = e$. Since $hg = g^{-1}(gh)g$ is a conjugate of $gh$,
the two have the same order. For the two transpositions, $gh$ and $hg$ are the two three-cycles (@exm-nonabelian-s3),
both of order $3$, although they are different elements.
:::

A power of an element has an order determined by the order of the element and the exponent. The third exercise
derives the formula and recovers the pattern found for $\mathbb{Z}_{12}$.

::: {#exr-grp-order-power}
#### The order of a power

Let $g$ have finite order $n$. Show that $g^m = e$ exactly when $n \mid m$, and that $g^k$ has order $n/\gcd(n, k)$.
How many elements of a cyclic group of order $n$ have order $n$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Write $m = qn + r$ with $0 \le r < n$; then $g^m = (g^n)^qg^r = g^r$, which is $e$ only if $r = 0$ by minimality of $n$.
With $d = \gcd(n, k)$, $(g^k)^m = e$ iff $n \mid km$ iff $(n/d) \mid (k/d)m$ iff $(n/d) \mid m$, because $n/d$ and
$k/d$ are coprime; so the order of $g^k$ is $n/d$. In a cyclic group $\langle g \rangle$ of order $n$ the element $g^k$
has order $n$ exactly when $\gcd(n, k) = 1$, which happens for $\varphi(n)$ values of $k$; in $\mathbb{Z}_{12}$ these are
$1, 5, 7, 11$ (@exr-grp-orders-z12).
:::
::::

### Subgroups

Inside a group there are often smaller sets of elements that are groups by themselves, such as the rotations among
all the symmetries of a triangle. The next definition makes this precise.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-subgroup}
#### Subgroup

A **subgroup** $H \subseteq G$ is a subset closed under multiplication and inverses (hence containing $e$); it is
a group with the restricted multiplication, written $H \leq G$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
For $\mathbb{Z}_6$ the subgroups are found by closing small sets under addition. The example shows two subgroups and
one subset that fails to be a subgroup.

::: {#exm-subgroup-z6}
#### Subgroups of $\mathbb{Z}_6$

$\{0, 2, 4\}$ and $\{0, 3\}$ are subgroups of $\mathbb{Z}_6$, closed under addition modulo $6$; $\{0, 1\}$ is not,
since $1 + 1 = 2$ is missing. The subgroups of $\mathbb{Z}_6$ have orders $1, 2, 3, 6$ (@exr-subgroups-s3).
:::

The symmetric group has subgroups of two different shapes. Each transposition together with the identity forms a
subgroup of order two, and the three-cycles together with the identity form a subgroup of order three.

::: {#exm-subgroup-s3}
#### Subgroups of $S_3$

$\{e, (1\,2)\}$, $\{e, (1\,3)\}$, $\{e, (2\,3)\}$ and $A_3 = \{e, (1\,2\,3), (1\,3\,2)\}$ are the proper non-trivial
subgroups of $S_3$ (@exr-subgroups-s3); $A_3$, the even permutations, is the **alternating group**, of order
$3$ (@prp-s3-facts).
:::

Among the infinite groups the most important subgroups are the rotations about a fixed axis. The example also names
the subgroups that later describe the sphere as a quotient.

::: {#exm-subgroup-so2}
#### $SO(2) \subset SO(3)$ and $U(1) \subset SU(2)$

The rotations about the $Z$-axis form a subgroup $SO(2)$ of $SO(3)$; the matrices $e^{tT_3} =
\operatorname{diag}(e^{-it/2}, e^{it/2})$ form a subgroup $U(1)$ of $SU(2)$. These are the subgroups by which
the sphere is a quotient, $S^2 = SO(3)/SO(2) \cong SU(2)/U(1)$ (@sec-coset-spaces).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The subgroups of a small group can be listed exhaustively, and the list reveals which subsets are closed. The first
exercise does this for $S_3$ and $\mathbb{Z}_6$ with Sage.

::: {#exr-subgroups-s3}
#### Subgroups of $S_3$ and $\mathbb{Z}_6$

List all subgroups of $S_3$ with their orders, decide which are normal, and compare the orders of the subgroups
of $\mathbb{Z}_6$ with the divisors of $6$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
{{< sage exr-subgroups-s3 >}}
:::

Checking closure under products and under inverses separately is often more work than needed. The second exercise
derives a one-step test and applies it to an infinite discrete group and to a group of rotations.

::: {#exr-grp-subgroup-test}
#### The one-step subgroup test

Show that a non-empty subset $H$ of a group is a subgroup exactly when $gh^{-1} \in H$ for all $g, h \in H$. Use the
test to show that the multiples $n\mathbb{Z}$ form a subgroup of $(\mathbb{Z}, +)$ and that the rotations $R(\alpha)$
form a subgroup of $GL(2, \mathbb{R})$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
A subgroup clearly passes the test. Conversely, take any $h \in H$: then $hh^{-1} = e \in H$, next $eh^{-1} = h^{-1}
\in H$, and finally $g(h^{-1})^{-1} = gh \in H$; so $H$ contains $e$ and is closed under inverses and products. In
additive notation the test reads $a - b \in H$, and $an - bn = (a - b)n \in n\mathbb{Z}$. For rotations
$R(\alpha)R(\beta)^{-1} = R(\alpha)R(-\beta) = R(\alpha - \beta)$ is again a rotation.
:::

Groups of order eight already have a rich collection of subgroups. The third exercise lists those of the symmetry
group of a square and sorts them by order and by whether they are cyclic.

::: {#exr-grp-subgroups-d4}
#### Subgroups of the symmetries of a square

The dihedral group $D_4$ consists of the four rotations and four reflections of a square, acting on its vertices
$1, 2, 3, 4$. List its subgroups with Sage, sort them by order, and describe the three subgroups of order $4$
geometrically.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
There are ten subgroups: the trivial one, five of order $2$ (the half turn and the four reflections, each with $e$),
three of order $4$ and $D_4$ itself. The subgroups of order $4$ are the rotations $\{e, r, r^2, r^3\}$, which is cyclic,
and two non-cyclic ones: the half turn with the two diagonal reflections, and the half turn with the two reflections
through the midpoints of opposite edges. Every order divides $8$:

{{< sage exr-grp-subgroups-d4 >}}
:::
::::

A subgroup can be described by listing its elements, or more economically by a few elements from which all others
are obtained by multiplication. The next definition names the subgroup reached this way.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-generated-subgroup}
#### Generated subgroup

The subgroup **generated** by elements $g_1, \dots, g_k$, written $\langle g_1, \dots, g_k \rangle$, is the
smallest subgroup containing them: the set of all finite products of the $g_i$ and their inverses. A group
generated by one element is **cyclic**.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
In $\mathbb{Z}_6$ the subgroup generated by one element consists of its multiples. The example finds which elements
generate the whole group and which generate proper subgroups.

::: {#exm-generated-z6}
#### Cyclic subgroups of $\mathbb{Z}_6$

$\langle 2 \rangle = \{0, 2, 4\}$ and $\langle 3 \rangle = \{0, 3\}$; $\langle 1 \rangle = \langle 5 \rangle =
\mathbb{Z}_6$. A cyclic subgroup $\langle g \rangle$ has order equal to the order of $g$.
:::

The symmetric group is not cyclic, since no element has order six, but two elements suffice. The example compares
the subgroups generated by one and by two permutations.

::: {#exm-generated-s3}
#### Generators of $S_3$

$\langle (1\,2\,3) \rangle = A_3$ and $\langle (1\,2) \rangle = \{e, (1\,2)\}$ (@exr-subgroups-s3), while
$\langle (1\,2), (1\,2\,3) \rangle = S_3$: the two generators of @fig-cayley-graph reach every element.
:::

In a continuous group a single element generates only a discrete set of powers. Whole circles of rotations need a
different kind of generator, which the example introduces.

::: {#exm-generated-rotations}
#### One-parameter subgroups

In $SO(2)$ the rotation by $60^\circ$ generates a cyclic subgroup of order $6$, a copy of $\mathbb{Z}_6$; in $SO(3)$
the rotations $R(t)$ about a fixed axis form the subgroup $SO(2)$, which is not generated by finitely many
elements but by the Lie algebra element $L_3$ through the exponential map (@sec-exponential).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Which elements generate a cyclic group is decided by the order formula of @exr-grp-order-power. The first exercise
lists the cyclic subgroups of $\mathbb{Z}_{12}$ and its generators.

::: {#exr-grp-generators-zn}
#### Generators of $\mathbb{Z}_{12}$

Compute $\langle k \rangle$ for every $k \in \mathbb{Z}_{12}$, find the elements that generate $\mathbb{Z}_{12}$, and
show that there is exactly one cyclic subgroup for each divisor of $12$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\langle k \rangle$ consists of the multiples of $\gcd(k, 12)$ and has $12/\gcd(k, 12)$ elements; it is all of
$\mathbb{Z}_{12}$ exactly for $k = 1, 5, 7, 11$. The distinct subgroups are $\langle d \rangle$ for the divisors $d = 1,
2, 3, 4, 6, 12$ (with $\langle 12 \rangle = \langle 0 \rangle = \{0\}$), of orders $12, 6, 4, 3, 2, 1$:

{{< sage exr-grp-generators-zn >}}
:::

Two well-chosen permutations can generate a large group, while other pairs generate only a small one. The second
exercise explores this in $S_4$, the group of order $24$ of permutations of four objects.

::: {#exr-grp-generated-s4}
#### Generating subgroups of $S_4$

With Sage, find the orders of $\langle (1\,2), (1\,2\,3\,4) \rangle$, $\langle (1\,2)(3\,4), (1\,3)(2\,4) \rangle$,
$\langle (1\,2\,3\,4) \rangle$ and $\langle (1\,2\,3), (1\,2)(3\,4) \rangle$ in $S_4$, and decide which of them are
cyclic or abelian.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
A transposition and a four-cycle generate all of $S_4$ (order $24$). The two double transpositions generate the
**Klein four-group** $\{e, (1\,2)(3\,4), (1\,3)(2\,4), (1\,4)(2\,3)\}$, abelian of order $4$ but not cyclic, since every
element other than $e$ has order $2$. The four-cycle generates a cyclic group of order $4$, and a three-cycle with a
double transposition generates the even permutations $A_4$, of order $12$:

{{< sage exr-grp-generated-s4 >}}
:::

Cyclic groups have the simplest possible subgroup structure, and the computation for $\mathbb{Z}_{12}$ is an instance
of a general theorem. The third exercise proves it.

::: {#exr-grp-cyclic-subgroups}
#### Subgroups of cyclic groups

Show that every subgroup of a cyclic group $\langle g \rangle$ of order $n$ is cyclic, generated by $g^m$ for the
least $m > 0$ with $g^m$ in the subgroup, and that $m$ divides $n$. Deduce that $\mathbb{Z}_n$ has exactly one
subgroup of each order dividing $n$, and list the subgroups of $\mathbb{Z}_6$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Let $H$ be a non-trivial subgroup and $m$ the least positive exponent with $g^m \in H$. For $g^k \in H$ write $k = qm +
r$ with $0 \le r < m$; then $g^r = g^k(g^m)^{-q} \in H$, so $r = 0$ by minimality and $g^k \in \langle g^m \rangle$. Hence
$H = \langle g^m \rangle$. Since $g^n = e \in H$, the same argument gives $m \mid n$, and $\langle g^m \rangle$ has
order $n/m$ (@exr-grp-order-power). So the subgroups correspond to the divisors $m$ of $n$, one of each order $n/m$.
For $\mathbb{Z}_6$: $\langle 1 \rangle = \mathbb{Z}_6$, $\langle 2 \rangle = \{0, 2, 4\}$, $\langle 3 \rangle = \{0,
3\}$ and $\langle 0 \rangle = \{0\}$.
:::
::::

Conjugating a subgroup by an element of the group, $h \mapsto ghg^{-1}$, produces another subgroup, which may or may
not be the original one. Subgroups that are carried to themselves by every conjugation are the ones by which a group
can be divided, and the next definition names them.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-normal-subgroup}
#### Normal subgroup

A subgroup $H$ is **normal** in $G$, written $H \trianglelefteq G$, if $gHg^{-1} = H$ for every $g \in G$, that
is, if $ghg^{-1} \in H$ whenever $h \in H$. Every subgroup of an abelian group is normal.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The even permutations form a normal subgroup of $S_3$, because conjugation does not change whether a permutation is
even. The example records this and points ahead to the quotient it allows.

::: {#exm-normal-a3}
#### $A_3$ is normal in $S_3$

Conjugating an even permutation gives an even permutation, so $gA_3g^{-1} = A_3$ (@exr-subgroups-s3); normality
of $A_3$ is what makes the quotient $S_3/A_3$ a group in @sec-cosets-quotients.
:::

A subgroup generated by a single transposition is moved by conjugation to the subgroup of another transposition. The
example computes one such conjugate and finds the same phenomenon among rotations.

::: {#exm-normal-not}
#### $\{e, (1\,2)\}$ is not normal

$(1\,3)(1\,2)(1\,3)^{-1} = (2\,3) \notin \{e, (1\,2)\}$: conjugation moves the transposition to another one. In
$SO(3)$ the subgroup $SO(2)$ of rotations about the $Z$-axis is not normal, since conjugating by a rotation about
$X$ tilts the axis; the sphere $SO(3)/SO(2)$ is therefore a set with a group action but not a group.
:::

The elements that commute with everything are fixed by every conjugation, so together they form a normal subgroup.
The example computes this subgroup for $SU(2)$ and for $S_3$.

::: {#exm-normal-centre}
#### The centre

The **centre** $\{z : zg = gz \text{ for all } g\}$ is always a normal subgroup; the centre of $SU(2)$ is $\{\pm 1\}$,
and $SU(2)/\{\pm 1\} \cong SO(3)$ (@sec-homomorphisms). The centre of $S_3$ is trivial.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Normality can be tested element by element, but for a group of order $24$ it is quicker to let Sage list the normal
subgroups. The first exercise does this for $S_4$ and finds a subgroup of order $4$ that is not normal.

::: {#exr-grp-normal-s4}
#### Normal subgroups of $S_4$

List the orders of the normal subgroups of $S_4$, identify the normal subgroup of order $4$, and show that the cyclic
subgroup $\langle (1\,2\,3\,4) \rangle$, also of order $4$, is not normal by exhibiting a conjugate that leaves it.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The normal subgroups have orders $1, 4, 12, 24$: the trivial group, the Klein four-group $\{e, (1\,2)(3\,4),
(1\,3)(2\,4), (1\,4)(2\,3)\}$ of @exr-grp-generated-s4, the alternating group $A_4$ and $S_4$. The Klein four-group is
normal because conjugation preserves the cycle type and it contains all three double transpositions. Conjugating the
four-cycle $(1\,2\,3\,4)$ by $(1\,2)$ gives the four-cycle $(1\,3\,4\,2)$, which is not a power of $(1\,2\,3\,4)$:

{{< sage exr-grp-normal-s4 >}}
:::

Matrix groups provide normal subgroups defined by an equation that conjugation preserves. The second exercise uses the
multiplicativity of the determinant, and the triangular matrices of @exr-grp-commutator, to decide normality without
computing conjugates one by one.

::: {#exr-grp-normal-det}
#### Normal subgroups of matrix groups

Show that $SL(n, \mathbb{R}) = \{A : \det A = 1\}$ is normal in $GL(n, \mathbb{R})$ and that $SO(n)$ is normal in
$O(n)$. In the group of invertible upper triangular $2 \times 2$ matrices, show that the matrices with both diagonal
entries $1$ form a normal subgroup while the diagonal matrices do not.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\det(gAg^{-1}) = \det g\det A(\det g)^{-1} = \det A$, so a conjugate of a matrix of determinant $1$ has determinant $1$;
the same argument with $SO(n) = O(n) \cap SL(n, \mathbb{R})$ gives the second statement. Conjugating $\begin{pmatrix} 1
& b \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ by an upper triangular matrix keeps the diagonal entries, which are the products of the
diagonal entries of the factors, so the result has diagonal $1, 1$ again: the subgroup is normal. Conjugating the
diagonal matrix $g = \operatorname{diag}(a, 1)$ by $h = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & b \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ gives $hgh^{-1} =
\begin{pmatrix} a & (1 - a)b \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$, which is not diagonal for $a \neq 1$, $b \neq 0$.
:::

The centre is always normal, but its size varies widely from group to group. The third exercise computes it for five
groups with Sage and explains each answer.

::: {#exr-grp-centre}
#### Centres of small groups

Compute the centres of $S_3$, $D_4$, $Q_8$, $S_4$ and $\mathbb{Z}_6$, check that each is a normal subgroup, and
describe the non-trivial ones.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$S_3$ and $S_4$ have trivial centre. The centre of $D_4$ is $\{e, r^2\}$, the half turn $(1\,3)(2\,4)$, which commutes
with every rotation and every reflection of the square; the centre of $Q_8$ is $\{\pm 1\}$; $\mathbb{Z}_6$ is abelian
and is its own centre. Each centre is normal since $gzg^{-1} = zgg^{-1} = z$:

{{< sage exr-grp-centre >}}
:::
::::

The notions of this section can now be summarised for the smallest non-abelian group. The proposition below collects
the basic facts about $S_3$: its order, its failure to commute, the orders of its elements and its alternating subgroup.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-s3-facts}
#### Facts about $S_3$

$S_3$ has six elements and is not abelian; a transposition has order $2$ and a three-cycle order $3$; the
alternating group $A_3$ has three elements.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** `KaluzaKlein.Groups.card_s3`, `KaluzaKlein.Groups.s3_not_comm`, `KaluzaKlein.Groups.transposition_order`,
`KaluzaKlein.Groups.three_cycle_order` and `KaluzaKlein.Groups.card_a3`, proved by exhaustive computation on the
permutations of three letters.

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.Groups.s3_not_comm >}}

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The abstract facts have a concrete picture in the symmetries of an equilateral triangle. Labelling the vertices $1, 2,
3$, every symmetry permutes the labels, and every permutation arises from exactly one symmetry.

::: {#exm-grp-s3-triangle}
#### The symmetries of a triangle

The rotations by $120^\circ$ and $240^\circ$ act on the vertices as the three-cycles, and they have order $3$; the
three reflections in the axes through a vertex act as the transpositions, each fixing one vertex, and have order
$2$. Rotating and then reflecting differs from reflecting and then rotating, which is the non-commutativity of
@prp-s3-facts seen with a paper triangle.
:::

The alternating group of the proposition is the subgroup of rotations of the triangle. Its three elements are the
powers of a single three-cycle, so it has the multiplication table of addition modulo $3$.

::: {#exm-grp-s3-alternating}
#### $A_3$ is cyclic of order three

$A_3 = \{e, (1\,2\,3), (1\,2\,3)^2\}$ with $(1\,2\,3)^2 = (1\,3\,2)$ and $(1\,2\,3)^3 = e$; sending $(1\,2\,3)^k$ to $k
\in \mathbb{Z}_3$ matches the two multiplication tables. It is abelian although $S_3$ is not, and it is the subgroup
generated by the three-cycle (@exm-generated-s3).
:::

The facts about $S_3$ are the case $n = 3$ of statements about every symmetric group. The example states the general
pattern, which the third exercise below checks for $n = 4$.

::: {#exm-grp-sn-facts}
#### The symmetric groups $S_n$

$S_n$ has $n!$ elements, since a permutation chooses an image for $1$ in $n$ ways, then for $2$ in $n - 1$ ways, and so
on; it is non-abelian for $n \ge 3$, because $(1\,2)$ and $(1\,3)$ do not commute. A $k$-cycle has order $k$, and the
even permutations form the alternating group $A_n$ with $n!/2$ elements; for $n = 4$ these numbers are $24$ and $12$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The proposition was verified one fact at a time; the full multiplication table shows all of them at once. The first
exercise prints the table with Sage and reads off the orders and the failure of commutativity.

::: {#exr-s3-table}
#### The multiplication table of $S_3$

With Sage's `SymmetricGroup`, list the elements of $S_3$ with their orders, check that $(1\,2)(1\,3) \neq
(1\,3)(1\,2)$, and print the multiplication table.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Sage composes permutations left to right, $(s t)(i) = t(s(i))$, so its products are the reverse of the
right-to-left convention of the text; either way the two products differ:

{{< sage exr-s3-table >}}

:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** The order of a three-cycle (@prp-s3-facts).

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.Groups.three_cycle_order >}}

**Sage.** The computation in the solution above.
:::

The six elements of $S_3$ can all be written in terms of one transposition and one three-cycle, subject to three
relations. The second exercise derives these relations by composing permutations by hand.

::: {#exr-grp-s3-presentation}
#### Generators and relations of $S_3$

With $s = (1\,2)$ and $c = (1\,2\,3)$, and products read right to left, show that $s^2 = e$, $c^3 = e$ and $scs^{-1} =
c^{-1}$. Write every element of $S_3$ in the form $c^is^j$ with $i \in \{0, 1, 2\}$, $j \in \{0, 1\}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$s^2 = e$ and $c^3 = e$ are the orders of @prp-s3-facts. For $scs$ (note $s^{-1} = s$), follow each label from the
right: $1 \mapsto 2 \mapsto 3 \mapsto 3$, $3 \mapsto 3 \mapsto 1 \mapsto 2$, $2 \mapsto 1 \mapsto 2 \mapsto 1$, so $scs$
sends $1 \to 3 \to 2 \to 1$ and equals $(1\,3\,2) = c^{-1}$. The six products are $e$, $c = (1\,2\,3)$, $c^2 =
(1\,3\,2)$, $s = (1\,2)$, $cs = (1\,3)$ (since $1 \mapsto 2 \mapsto 3$, $3 \mapsto 3 \mapsto 1$, $2 \mapsto 1 \mapsto
2$) and $c^2s = (2\,3)$. The relation $sc = c^{-1}s$ lets any word in $s$ and $c$ be brought to this form.
:::

The general pattern of @exm-grp-sn-facts can be checked on the next symmetric group. The third exercise sorts the
elements of $S_4$ by cycle type and order.

::: {#exr-grp-s4-facts}
#### The same facts for $S_4$

With Sage, check that $|S_4| = 24$, sort its elements by cycle type, give the order of each type, and find $|A_4|$.
Which orders occur, and do they all divide $24$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
There are $1$ identity, $6$ transpositions and $3$ double transpositions of order $2$, $8$ three-cycles of order $3$
and $6$ four-cycles of order $4$, in all $24$ elements. The order of a permutation is the least common multiple of its
cycle lengths, so a double transposition has order $2$, not $4$. The orders $1, 2, 3, 4$ all divide $24$, and the even
permutations (identity, double transpositions, three-cycles) number $1 + 3 + 8 = 12$:

{{< sage exr-grp-s4-facts >}}
:::
::::

## Cosets and quotient groups {#sec-cosets-quotients}

A subgroup slices a group into cosets, equal-sized pieces that the group permutes. When the subgroup is normal the
set of cosets is again a group; when it is not, it is still a set on which the group acts, and the coset spaces
of @sec-coset-spaces, including the sphere $SO(3)/SO(2)$, are exactly these sets with a manifold structure. This
section defines cosets, proves Lagrange's theorem, and introduces quotient groups, group actions, orbits and
stabilisers.

### Cosets

Multiplying every element of a subgroup by a fixed element $g$ produces a translated copy of the subgroup. These
translated copies, and the way they partition the group, are the subject of the definition below.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-left-coset}
#### Left coset

For a subgroup $H$ of $G$ the **left coset** of $g$ is the set $gH = \{gh : h \in H\}$; the **right coset** is
$Hg = \{hg : h \in H\}$. Two left cosets are either equal or disjoint, since $gH \cap g'H \neq \emptyset$ implies
$g^{-1}g' \in H$ and then $g'H = gH$: "$g \sim g'$ iff $g^{-1}g' \in H$" is an equivalence relation
(@def-equivalence-relation) whose classes are the left cosets, and the set of left cosets is the quotient set
(@def-quotient-set), written $G/H$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The simplest cosets are translates in an abelian group. In $\mathbb{Z}_6$ the subgroup of even residues has exactly one
translate besides itself, the odd residues.

::: {#exm-cosets-z6}
#### $\mathbb{Z}_6 / \{0, 2, 4\}$

With $H = \{0, 2, 4\}$ in $\mathbb{Z}_6$ the cosets are $0 + H = \{0, 2, 4\}$ and $1 + H = \{1, 3, 5\}$, the even
and odd residues (@fig-coset-z6, @prp-z6-cosets); $2 + H = H$ again. In an abelian group left and right cosets
coincide.
:::

![The cosets of $H = \{0, 2, 4\}$ in $\mathbb{Z}_6$, drawn on the hexagon of rotations by multiples of $60^\circ$:
the two triangles are the two cosets, and the quotient $\mathbb{Z}_6/H = \mathbb{Z}_2$ swaps them. Generated by
`figures/coset_z6.sage`.](figures/coset_z6.svg){#fig-coset-z6 width=40%}

In a non-abelian group the left and right translates of a subgroup can be different sets. The example compares them
for a normal and for a non-normal subgroup of $S_3$, with products read right to left.

::: {#exm-cosets-s3}
#### Cosets in $S_3$

For $A_3$ the left cosets are $A_3$ and the odd permutations $\{(1\,2), (1\,3), (2\,3)\}$, the same as the right
cosets. For $H = \{e, (1\,2)\}$ the three left cosets are $\{e, (1\,2)\}$, $\{(1\,2\,3), (1\,3)\}$, $\{(1\,3\,2),
(2\,3)\}$ and the right cosets $\{e, (1\,2)\}$, $\{(1\,2\,3), (2\,3)\}$, $\{(1\,3\,2), (1\,3)\}$ differ
(@exr-s3-cosets): left and right cosets agree exactly when the subgroup is normal.
:::

For an infinite group the cosets can form a continuum, and they can carry a geometric meaning. The cosets of the
rotations about one axis are labelled by the points of the sphere.

::: {#exm-cosets-so3}
#### Cosets of $SO(2)$ in $SO(3)$

Let $H = SO(2)$ be the rotations about the $Z$-axis. Two rotations $g, g'$ lie in the same left coset exactly when
$g^{-1}g'$ fixes the $Z$-axis, that is, when $g$ and $g'$ send the north pole $o = (0, 0, 1)$ to the same point
(@exm-equivalence-coset). So the coset $gH$ is labelled by the point $g \cdot o$ of the sphere, every point
arises, and $SO(3)/SO(2) \cong S^2$ as sets (@exr-so3-coset-set); @sec-coset-spaces makes this a diffeomorphism.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The cosets in $S_3$ are small enough to compute by hand and to check with Sage. The first exercise asks for both
kinds of cosets of the two subgroups of the example, and for the quotient when there is one.

::: {#exr-s3-cosets}
#### Cosets in $S_3$

List the left and right cosets of $A_3$ and of $H = \{e, (1\,2)\}$ in $S_3$; decide which subgroup is normal and
identify the quotient group when it exists.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$A_3 = \{e, (1\,2\,3), (1\,3\,2)\}$; its left and right cosets both are $A_3$ and the odd permutations
$\{(1\,2), (1\,3), (2\,3)\}$, so $A_3$ is normal and $S_3/A_3 \cong \mathbb{Z}_2$. For $H$ the left cosets are
$\{e, (1\,2)\}, \{(1\,2\,3), (1\,3)\}, \{(1\,3\,2), (2\,3)\}$ and the right cosets $\{e, (1\,2)\}, \{(1\,2\,3), (2\,3)\},
\{(1\,3\,2), (1\,3)\}$; they differ, $H$ is not normal, and $S_3/H$ is a three-element set. Sage composes
permutations left to right, so the cosets it calls left are the right cosets of the text. In Sage:

{{< sage exr-s3-cosets >}}
:::

The identification of the cosets of $SO(2)$ with the points of the sphere deserves a proof. The second exercise
gives it, using only that rotations act on unit vectors.

::: {#exr-so3-coset-set}
#### Cosets of $SO(2)$ in $SO(3)$

Show that two rotations lie in the same left coset of $SO(2) = \{$rotations about $Z\}$ exactly when they map the
north pole to the same point, and that the map $gSO(2) \mapsto g \cdot (0,0,1)$ is a bijection onto the sphere.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$g' \in gSO(2)$ iff $g^{-1}g' \in SO(2)$ iff $g^{-1}g'$ fixes $o = (0,0,1)$ iff $g' \cdot o = g \cdot o$. The map
is therefore well defined and injective; it is surjective because every unit vector is the image of $o$ under some
rotation (rotate about the axis perpendicular to $o$ and the target). This is the orbit-stabiliser bijection of
@def-stabiliser, and the decomposition of $\mathfrak{so}(3)$ in @sec-reductive is its infinitesimal version.
:::

In a cyclic group of composite order there are several subgroups and therefore several ways to slice the group. The
third exercise slices $\mathbb{Z}_{12}$ in two of them.

::: {#exr-cosq-cosets-z12}
#### Cosets in $\mathbb{Z}_{12}$

List the cosets of $\langle 4 \rangle = \{0, 4, 8\}$ and of $\langle 3 \rangle = \{0, 3, 6, 9\}$ in $\mathbb{Z}_{12}$,
check that each family partitions the group, and compare the number of cosets with $12/|H|$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The cosets of $\langle 4 \rangle$ are the four residue classes modulo $4$, $\{0, 4, 8\}, \{1, 5, 9\}, \{2, 6, 10\},
\{3, 7, 11\}$; those of $\langle 3 \rangle$ are the three classes modulo $3$, $\{0, 3, 6, 9\}, \{1, 4, 7, 10\}, \{2, 5,
8, 11\}$. In both cases the cosets are disjoint, have $|H|$ elements, and their number is $12/|H|$:

{{< sage exr-cosq-cosets-z12 >}}
:::
::::

The cosets of the examples all have the same size and fill the group without overlapping. For a finite group this
turns into a counting statement, the oldest theorem of group theory.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#thm-lagrange}
#### Lagrange's theorem

If $G$ is finite, every left coset has $|H|$ elements ($h \mapsto gh$ is a bijection $H \to gH$) and the cosets
partition $G$, so $|H|$ divides $|G|$; the number of cosets is the **index** $[G : H] = |G|/|H|$. In particular
the order of every element divides $|G|$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Proved in the text. The instance $A_3 \subseteq S_3$ is `KaluzaKlein.Groups.lagrange_a3` (its statement is shown
after @exr-lagrange).

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The theorem restricts the possible sizes of subgroups before any of them is computed. For $S_3$ the restriction leaves
only the orders that actually occur.

::: {#exm-lagrange-s3}
#### Subgroups of $S_3$

The subgroups of $S_3$ have orders $1, 2, 3, 6$, all divisors of $6$, and there is no subgroup of order $4$
(@exr-lagrange); $[S_3 : A_3] = 2$ and $[S_3 : \{e, (1\,2)\}] = 3$.
:::

When the order of a group is prime, Lagrange's theorem leaves almost no room. The example derives the complete
structure of such groups from it.

::: {#exm-lagrange-prime}
#### Groups of prime order

A group of prime order $p$ has no subgroups other than $\{e\}$ and itself, and every element other than $e$
generates it: every group of prime order is cyclic, $\cong \mathbb{Z}_p$.
:::

For infinite groups the counting loses its meaning, but a version of it survives for groups of rotations. The example
replaces the count of cosets by a count of dimensions.

::: {#exm-lagrange-infinite}
#### Infinite index

$SO(2) \subset SO(3)$ has infinitely many cosets, one per point of the sphere; Lagrange's counting is replaced by
a counting of dimensions, $\dim SO(3)/SO(2) = 3 - 1 = 2$ (@sec-coset-spaces).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The theorem excludes some subgroups at once. The first exercise uses it to rule out a subgroup of order $4$ in $S_3$
and then lists the subgroups that remain.

::: {#exr-lagrange}
#### Lagrange's theorem

Show that $S_3$ has no subgroup of order $4$, and list its subgroups by order.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
By Lagrange's theorem the order of a subgroup divides $6$, so the possible orders are $1, 2, 3, 6$: the trivial
group; three subgroups of order $2$ generated by the transpositions; one of order $3$, $A_3$; and $S_3$ itself.
A subgroup of order $4$ is impossible since $4 \nmid 6$.

:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** The instance $|A_3| = 3$ divides $|S_3| = 6$ of Lagrange's theorem.

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.Groups.lagrange_a3 >}}

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Applied to the group of non-zero residues modulo a prime, Lagrange's theorem becomes a classical statement of number
theory. The second exercise derives it and its generalisation to any modulus.

::: {#exr-cosq-fermat}
#### Fermat's little theorem

Show that $g^{|G|} = e$ for every element of a finite group. Apply this to the group of non-zero residues modulo a
prime $p$ (@exr-grp-units-mod5) to prove $a^{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod p$ for $p \nmid a$, and to the residues coprime to $n$
to prove $a^{\varphi(n)} \equiv 1 \pmod n$. Check $2^4 \bmod 5$ and $5^2 \bmod 6$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The order $m$ of $g$ is the order of $\langle g \rangle$, which divides $|G|$ by Lagrange's theorem; so $|G| = mk$ and
$g^{|G|} = (g^m)^k = e$. The non-zero residues modulo $p$ form a group of order $p - 1$ under multiplication, so
$a^{p-1} = 1$ in it. The residues coprime to $n$ are closed under multiplication and have inverses (by Bézout's
identity), forming a group of order $\varphi(n)$, whence $a^{\varphi(n)} \equiv 1$. Indeed $2^4 = 16 \equiv 1 \pmod 5$
and $5^2 = 25 \equiv 1 \pmod 6$, with $\varphi(6) = 2$.
:::

Lagrange's theorem says which orders are possible, not which orders occur. The third exercise shows with Sage that the
converse fails already for a group of order $12$.

::: {#exr-cosq-a4-no-6}
#### The converse of Lagrange's theorem fails

Show that the alternating group $A_4$, of order $12$, has subgroups of orders $1, 2, 3, 4, 12$ but none of order $6$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$A_4$ consists of the identity, three double transpositions and eight three-cycles. A subgroup of order $6$ would have
index $2$. A subgroup of index $2$ is normal, since its left and right cosets are both $H$ and its complement; its two
cosets then multiply like $\mathbb{Z}_2$ (@def-quotient-group), so it contains the square of every element; and every three-cycle is the square of a three-cycle, so it would contain all eight
three-cycles, too many for six elements. Sage confirms the list of subgroup orders:

{{< sage exr-cosq-a4-no-6 >}}
:::
::::

### Quotient groups

For the even and odd residues of $\mathbb{Z}_6$, adding any even number to any odd number gives an odd number, so the
cosets themselves can be added. The definition below says when such a multiplication of cosets is possible.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-quotient-group}
#### Quotient group

When $H$ is normal, the product of cosets $gH \cdot g'H = gg'H$ is well defined (it does not depend on the
representatives, because $g'H = Hg'$), and makes $G/H$ a group, the **quotient group**, with identity $H$ and
inverse $(gH)^{-1} = g^{-1}H$. The quotient map $g \mapsto gH$ is a homomorphism (@sec-homomorphisms).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The parity rule for sums is the multiplication of the quotient group of $\mathbb{Z}_6$ by its even residues. The example
writes it out and states the general pattern for cyclic groups.

::: {#exm-quotient-z6-z2}
#### $\mathbb{Z}_6/\{0, 2, 4\} \cong \mathbb{Z}_2$

The two cosets of @exm-cosets-z6 add by parity: even plus even is even, even plus odd is odd, odd plus odd is even
(@prp-z6-cosets). The quotient is $\mathbb{Z}_2$, and in general $\mathbb{Z}_n/\langle d \rangle \cong \mathbb{Z}_d$
for $d \mid n$.
:::

The same parity rule holds for permutations, with even and odd now referring to the number of transpositions. The
example identifies the quotient of $S_3$ by its normal subgroup $A_3$.

::: {#exm-quotient-s3-a3}
#### $S_3/A_3 \cong \mathbb{Z}_2$

$A_3$ is normal, and its two cosets, the even and the odd permutations, multiply as the signs $\pm 1$:
$S_3/A_3$ is the group $\{+1, -1\}$ of the sign of a permutation (@exr-s3-cosets, @sec-homomorphisms).
:::

Normality is not a technicality: without it the product of cosets depends on the chosen representatives. The example
shows the failure for the left cosets of a subgroup of order two, computed in @exm-cosets-s3.

::: {#exm-quotient-not-group}
#### $S_3/\{e, (1\,2)\}$ is not a group

For the non-normal subgroup $H = \{e, (1\,2)\}$ the product of cosets depends on the representatives: $(1\,2\,3)H
\cdot (1\,3\,2)H$ would be $eH$ using $(1\,2\,3)(1\,3\,2) = e$ but $(1\,3)(2\,3) = (1\,3\,2)$ lands in a different coset
using the other representatives. $S_3/H$ is a three-element set permuted by $S_3$, not a group; likewise
$SO(3)/SO(2)$ is a set, the sphere, not a group.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Every subgroup of $\mathbb{Z}_{12}$ is normal, so every slicing of @exr-cosq-cosets-z12 gives a quotient group. The first
exercise builds two of these quotients by hand and with Sage's `quotient`.

::: {#exr-cosq-quotient-z12}
#### Quotients of $\mathbb{Z}_{12}$

Show that the addition of cosets of $\langle 4 \rangle$ in $\mathbb{Z}_{12}$ is well defined and that the quotient is
cyclic of order $4$, generated by the coset of $1$. Do the same for $\langle 6 \rangle$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The cosets of $\langle 4 \rangle$ are the classes modulo $4$, and the class of a sum depends only on the classes of the
summands because $4 \mid 12$. The coset $1 + \langle 4 \rangle$ has order $4$ in the quotient: $k + \langle 4 \rangle$
is the identity coset exactly when $4 \mid k$. So $\mathbb{Z}_{12}/\langle 4 \rangle$ has the table of
$\mathbb{Z}_4$, and likewise $\mathbb{Z}_{12}/\langle 6 \rangle$ has the table of $\mathbb{Z}_6$:

{{< sage exr-cosq-quotient-z12 >}}
:::

The definition asserts that normality makes the product of cosets well defined; the converse holds as well. The second
exercise proves both directions.

::: {#exr-cosq-well-defined}
#### When is the product of cosets well defined?

Show that the rule $gH \cdot g'H = gg'H$ is independent of the representatives when $H$ is normal. Conversely, show
that if the rule is independent of the representatives, then $H$ is normal.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
If $H$ is normal and $g_1 = gh_1$, $g_1' = g'h_2$ are other representatives, then $g_1g_1' = gh_1g'h_2 =
gg'(g'^{-1}h_1g')h_2$, and $g'^{-1}h_1g' \in H$, so $g_1g_1' \in gg'H$. Conversely, suppose the rule is well defined and
let $h \in H$, $g \in G$. Since $hH = eH$, the products $hH \cdot g^{-1}H = hg^{-1}H$ and $eH \cdot g^{-1}H = g^{-1}H$
must agree, so $(g^{-1})^{-1}hg^{-1} = ghg^{-1} \in H$: $H$ is normal.
:::

A quotient of a non-abelian group can be abelian, and the quotient by the centre measures how far a group is from
being abelian. The third exercise computes it for the symmetries of a square and proves a general consequence.

::: {#exr-cosq-quotient-d4}
#### The quotient of $D_4$ by its centre

Compute $D_4/Z$ for the centre $Z = \{e, r^2\}$ of @exr-grp-centre, decide whether it is cyclic, and prove that a group
$G$ whose quotient $G/Z(G)$ by its centre is cyclic must be abelian.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$D_4/Z$ has $8/2 = 4$ elements, each of order at most $2$ (the square of any element of $D_4$ is $e$ or $r^2$), so it
is the Klein four-group, abelian but not cyclic:

{{< sage exr-cosq-quotient-d4 >}}

If $G/Z(G)$ is generated by $aZ(G)$, every element is $a^kz$ with $z$ central, and $(a^kz)(a^lz') = a^{k+l}zz' =
(a^lz')(a^kz)$, so $G$ is abelian. This explains why the quotient of the non-abelian $D_4$ by its centre could not
be cyclic.
:::
::::

### Group actions, orbits and stabilisers

A group usually appears in practice as a set of transformations of something else: rotations move points, permutations
move labels. The next definition separates the group from the set it transforms.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-group-action}
#### Group action

A (left) **action** of $G$ on a set $X$ is a map $(g, x) \mapsto g \cdot x$ with $e \cdot x = x$ and $g \cdot (h
\cdot x) = (gh) \cdot x$; each $g$ then acts as a bijection of $X$. The action is **transitive** if any $x$ can
be moved to any $y$ by some $g$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Every subgroup produces an action, on its own cosets. The example describes this action and the two cases met so far.

::: {#exm-action-cosets}
#### Actions on cosets

$G$ acts on $G/H$ by $g \cdot (g'H) = gg'H$, transitively; for $H = \{e, (1\,2)\}$ this permutes the three cosets
of @exm-cosets-s3, and for $SO(2) \subset SO(3)$ it is the action of rotations on the sphere.
:::

Matrix groups act on the vectors they multiply, and permutation groups on the labels they permute. The example lists
these basic actions and their restrictions to invariant sets.

::: {#exm-action-rotations}
#### Rotations on space and on the sphere

$SO(3)$ acts on $\mathbb{R}^3$ by matrix multiplication, and on the sphere $S^2$ by restriction, transitively:
any unit vector can be rotated to any other. $S_3$ acts on $\{1, 2, 3\}$ by permuting, transitively
(@exr-orbit-stabiliser).
:::

A group can also act on itself, and not only by multiplication. Conjugation is the action that tests normality, and its
orbits sort the elements of a group into classes.

::: {#exm-action-conjugation}
#### Conjugation

$G$ acts on itself by **conjugation**, $g \cdot h = ghg^{-1}$; a subgroup is normal exactly when it is a union
of orbits of this action, and the orbits are the **conjugacy classes**: $\{e\}$, the three transpositions and
the two three-cycles in $S_3$ (@exr-s3-irreps).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The axiom $g \cdot (h \cdot x) = (gh) \cdot x$ fixes the order in which group elements act, and it is easy to violate.
The first exercise shows that multiplying on the right is not a left action unless an inverse is inserted.

::: {#exr-cosq-action-right}
#### Right multiplication

Show that $g \cdot x = xg$ does not define a left action of a non-abelian group $G$ on itself, but $g \cdot x = xg^{-1}$
does. Check the first claim on $S_3$ with $g = (1\,2)$, $h = (1\,3)$, $x = e$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $g \cdot x = xg$, $g \cdot (h \cdot x) = xhg$ while $(gh) \cdot x = xgh$; these differ whenever $gh \neq hg$, for
instance for $x = e$ and the two transpositions, whose products in the two orders are the two different three-cycles.
With $g \cdot x = xg^{-1}$, $g \cdot (h \cdot x) = xh^{-1}g^{-1} = x(gh)^{-1} = (gh) \cdot x$, and $e \cdot x = x$.
:::

A group that acts on a set also acts on the functions defined on it, and the inverse in the definition below is forced
by the same bookkeeping. The second exercise derives the correct formula and shows where the naive one fails.

::: {#exr-cosq-action-functions}
#### Actions on functions

Let $G = GL(2, \mathbb{R})$ act on $\mathbb{R}^2$ by matrix multiplication. Show that $(g \cdot f)(x) = f(g^{-1}x)$ is a
left action on functions $f : \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}$, while $(g \cdot f)(x) = f(gx)$ satisfies $g \cdot (h \cdot
f) = (hg) \cdot f$ instead. Why do both formulas give actions of the subgroup $SO(2)$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$(g \cdot (h \cdot f))(x) = (h \cdot f)(g^{-1}x) = f(h^{-1}g^{-1}x) = f((gh)^{-1}x) = ((gh) \cdot f)(x)$, and the identity
matrix acts trivially. With the other formula, $(g \cdot (h \cdot f))(x) = (h \cdot f)(gx) = f(hgx) = ((hg) \cdot f)(x)$,
so the order is reversed (a **right action**); for $f(x) = x_1$ and non-commuting $g, h$ the two sides differ. $SO(2)$
is abelian (@exm-abelian-zn), so $hg = gh$ and the distinction disappears.
:::

The action of a group on the cosets of a subgroup gives a permutation of the cosets for each group element. The third
exercise computes these permutations for $S_3$ acting on the three cosets of $\{e, (1\,2)\}$.

::: {#exr-cosq-action-perm}
#### $S_3$ permuting three cosets

Let $S_3$ act on the left cosets $C_0 = H$, $C_1 = (1\,3\,2)H$, $C_2 = (1\,2\,3)H$ of $H = \{e, (1\,2)\}$ by $g \cdot xH =
gxH$. Compute the permutation of $(C_0, C_1, C_2)$ induced by each $g$, verify the action axioms, and decide whether
different elements give different permutations.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The three-cycles permute the cosets cyclically, and each transposition fixes one coset and swaps the other two; for
instance $(1\,2)$ fixes $C_0 = H$. The six permutations are distinct, so this action reproduces $S_3$ as the full group
of permutations of three cosets. The Sage script uses the right-to-left product of the text, which is $x * g$ in Sage:

{{< sage exr-cosq-action-perm >}}
:::
::::

An action moves each point within a definite region of the set, the points it can reach. The next definition names
this region.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-orbit}
#### Orbit

The **orbit** of $x \in X$ is the set $G \cdot x = \{g \cdot x : g \in G\}$ of points reachable from $x$. Orbits
partition $X$ ("$x \sim y$ iff $y = g \cdot x$ for some $g$" is an equivalence relation), and the action is
transitive exactly when there is a single orbit.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Rotations preserve distances from the origin, so they cannot move a point off the sphere through it. The example
finds the orbits of the rotations of space and of the rotations about one axis.

::: {#exm-orbit-sphere}
#### Orbits of rotations

The orbits of $SO(3)$ on $\mathbb{R}^3$ are the spheres $|x| = r$ and the origin; the orbit of the north pole on
$S^2$ is the whole sphere. The orbits of $SO(2)$ (rotations about $Z$) on $S^2$ are the parallels and the two
poles, which is why fields on $S^2$ that are $SO(2)$-invariant depend only on $\theta$.
:::

One group can act on several sets with different numbers of orbits. The example lets $S_3$ act on points, on pairs of
points and on itself.

::: {#exm-orbit-s3}
#### Orbits of $S_3$

Acting on $\{1, 2, 3\}$, $S_3$ has one orbit; acting on pairs $\{i, j\}$ it has one orbit of three pairs; acting
on itself by conjugation it has three orbits, the conjugacy classes (@exr-orbit-stabiliser).
:::

Restricting an action to a subgroup can split orbits. The symmetries of a hexagon and two of its subgroups show
transitive and non-transitive actions on the same six vertices.

::: {#exm-orbit-hexagon}
#### The dihedral group

The symmetries of a regular hexagon, the **dihedral group** $D_6$ of order $12$, act on the six vertices with a
single orbit; the subgroup of rotations $\mathbb{Z}_6$ also acts transitively, and the reflection group
$\{e, \sigma\}$ in one axis has orbits of size $1$ and $2$ (@exr-orbit-stabiliser).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Sage computes orbits of permutation groups directly, both on points and on sets of points. The first exercise finds the
orbits of a cyclic group on six points and of $D_4$ on the vertices and on the pairs of vertices of a square.

::: {#exr-cosq-orbits}
#### Orbits with Sage

Find the orbits of the group generated by $(1\,2\,3)(4\,5)$ on $\{1, \dots, 6\}$. Then find the orbits of $D_4$ on the
four vertices of a square and on the six two-element sets of vertices, and interpret the latter geometrically.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The element $(1\,2\,3)(4\,5)$ has order $6$, and its powers move $1, 2, 3$ among themselves, swap $4, 5$ and fix $6$:
the orbits are $\{1, 2, 3\}, \{4, 5\}, \{6\}$, the cycles of the generator. $D_4$ is transitive on the vertices. On
pairs of vertices it has two orbits, the four edges and the two diagonals, since a symmetry preserves distances:

{{< sage exr-cosq-orbits >}}
:::

The definition states that orbits partition the set. The second exercise asks for the verification that the relation
"reachable from" is an equivalence relation, which uses each axiom of an action once.

::: {#exr-cosq-orbits-partition}
#### Orbits partition the set

Show that $x \sim y$ iff $y = g \cdot x$ for some $g$ is reflexive, symmetric and transitive, and deduce that two
orbits are either equal or disjoint. Which axiom of a group or of an action is used at each step?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Reflexive: $x = e \cdot x$, by the identity axiom of the action. Symmetric: if $y = g \cdot x$ then $g^{-1} \cdot y =
g^{-1} \cdot (g \cdot x) = (g^{-1}g) \cdot x = x$, using inverses and the compatibility axiom. Transitive: if $y = g \cdot
x$ and $z = h \cdot y$ then $z = h \cdot (g \cdot x) = (hg) \cdot x$, using compatibility and closure. The orbits are the
equivalence classes, and the classes of an equivalence relation are equal or disjoint (@def-equivalence-relation).
:::

Orbits of continuous groups are often curves or surfaces, and they sort the points of a space into families. The third
exercise compares the orbits of three groups acting on the plane and of the group that combines rotations and
dilations.

::: {#exr-cosq-orbits-plane}
#### Orbits in the plane

Describe the orbits on $\mathbb{R}^2$ of $SO(2)$ acting by rotations, of the positive reals acting by dilations $t \cdot x
= tx$, and of $(\mathbb{R}, +)$ acting by horizontal translations $a \cdot (x, y) = (x + a, y)$. Then let the non-zero
complex numbers act on $\mathbb{C} = \mathbb{R}^2$ by multiplication and find the orbits.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The rotation orbits are the circles about the origin and the origin itself; the dilation orbits are the open rays from
the origin and the origin; the translation orbits are the horizontal lines. A non-zero complex number $re^{i\alpha}$
rotates by $\alpha$ and dilates by $r$, so it can move any non-zero point to any other: there are two orbits, $\{0\}$
and $\mathbb{C} \setminus \{0\}$. Combining two groups merges their orbits, here circles and rays into the punctured
plane.
:::
::::

While an orbit records where a point can go, the elements that leave it in place form a subgroup. The next definition
names this subgroup and relates its cosets to the orbit.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-stabiliser}
#### Stabiliser

The **stabiliser** (or **isotropy group**) of $x$ is the subgroup $G_x = \{g : g \cdot x = x\}$. The map $gG_x
\mapsto g \cdot x$ is a bijection from the cosets $G/G_x$ onto the orbit $G \cdot x$ (**orbit-stabiliser
theorem**), so $|G| = |G \cdot x|\,|G_x|$ for finite $G$, and stabilisers of points in the same orbit are
conjugate, $G_{g \cdot x} = g G_x g^{-1}$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The rotations that fix the north pole are the rotations about the polar axis. The example identifies the sphere with
the cosets of this stabiliser, as in @exm-cosets-so3.

::: {#exm-stabiliser-so2}
#### The stabiliser of the north pole

The stabiliser of $o = (0, 0, 1)$ in $SO(3)$ is $SO(2)$, the rotations about the $Z$-axis, and the orbit-stabiliser
bijection $SO(3)/SO(2) \to S^2$ is @exm-cosets-so3. The stabiliser of any other point is the group of rotations
about the axis through it, a conjugate of $SO(2)$: this is the **isotropy group** of @sec-coset-spaces.
:::

For finite groups the orbit-stabiliser theorem is a counting formula: the order of the group is the size of an orbit
times the order of a stabiliser. The example checks it on two transitive actions.

::: {#exm-stabiliser-s3}
#### Stabilisers in $S_3$ and $D_6$

The stabiliser of $1$ in $S_3$ is $\{e, (2\,3)\}$, of order $2$, and $3 \cdot 2 = 6$; the stabiliser of a vertex
of the hexagon in $D_6$ is the reflection in the axis through that vertex, of order $2$, and $6 \cdot 2 = 12$
(@exr-orbit-stabiliser).
:::

At the other extreme from a large stabiliser is a trivial one. The example names the actions in which no element
other than the identity fixes any point.

::: {#exm-stabiliser-free}
#### Free actions

An action is **free** if every stabiliser is trivial; the action of $G$ on itself by left multiplication is free
and transitive, and the action of $U(1)$ on $SU(2) = S^3$ by right multiplication is free, its orbits being the
circles of the Hopf fibration (@sec-hopf) with quotient $S^2$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Sage computes orbits and stabilisers of permutation groups, so the counting formula can be checked mechanically. The
first exercise does this for $S_3$ and for the symmetries of a hexagon.

::: {#exr-orbit-stabiliser}
#### Orbits and stabilisers with Sage

Compute the orbit and stabiliser of $1$ under $S_3$ and of a vertex under the dihedral group $D_6$, check
$|G| = |\text{orbit}|\,|\text{stabiliser}|$, and verify that the cosets of the stabiliser correspond to the points
of the orbit.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
{{< sage exr-orbit-stabiliser >}}
:::

The last clause of the definition says that moving a point moves its stabiliser by conjugation. The second exercise
proves it and applies it to the rotations of the sphere.

::: {#exr-cosq-conjugate-stabiliser}
#### Stabilisers along an orbit

Prove that $G_{g \cdot x} = gG_xg^{-1}$, and deduce that all stabilisers along an orbit have the same order. Use the
formula to describe the stabiliser in $SO(3)$ of the point $(1, 0, 0)$ from that of the north pole.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
If $k \in G_x$ then $(gkg^{-1}) \cdot (g \cdot x) = g \cdot (k \cdot x) = g \cdot x$, so $gG_xg^{-1} \subseteq G_{g
\cdot x}$; applying this to the point $g \cdot x$ and the element $g^{-1}$ gives the reverse inclusion. Conjugation by
$g$ is a bijection, so the orders agree. A rotation $g$ by $90^\circ$ about the $Y$-axis sends $(0, 0, 1)$ to $(1, 0, 0)$
and conjugating the rotations about $Z$ by $g$ gives the rotations about $g$ applied to the $Z$-axis,
which is the $X$-axis: the stabiliser of $(1, 0, 0)$ is the group of rotations about $X$.
:::

The orbit-stabiliser theorem is an efficient way to count the symmetries of a solid. The third exercise counts the
rotations of a cube from one vertex and checks the count with a Sage matrix group.

::: {#exr-cosq-cube-rotations}
#### The rotations of a cube

Let $G$ be the group generated by the quarter turns about the $Z$- and $X$-axes acting on the cube with vertices $(\pm 1,
\pm 1, \pm 1)$. Find the orbit and the stabiliser of the vertex $(1, 1, 1)$ and of the face centre $(0, 0, 1)$, and
deduce $|G|$ in two ways.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Every vertex can be reached from $(1, 1, 1)$, so the orbit has $8$ points; the rotations fixing $(1, 1, 1)$ turn the
cube about the main diagonal by $0^\circ$, $120^\circ$ or $240^\circ$, cyclically permuting the coordinates, so the
stabiliser has order $3$ and $|G| = 8 \cdot 3 = 24$. The face centres form an orbit of $6$ points with stabiliser the
four rotations about the $Z$-axis, and $6 \cdot 4 = 24$ again. Sage's `MatrixGroup` confirms:

{{< sage exr-cosq-cube-rotations >}}
:::
::::

The cosets of the even residues in $\mathbb{Z}_6$ have been the running example of this section. The proposition below
records their computation, which amounts to a finite check on the six residues and the thirty-six pairs of them.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-z6-cosets}
#### The cosets and quotient of $\mathbb{Z}_6$ by $\{0, 2, 4\}$

The cosets $0 + H$ and $1 + H$ are $\{0, 2, 4\}$ and $\{1, 3, 5\}$ and partition $\mathbb{Z}_6$; the coset of a sum
depends only on the cosets of the summands (parity).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** `KaluzaKlein.Groups.zmod6_cosets` and `KaluzaKlein.Groups.zmod6_quotient`, proved by exhaustive computation on
`ZMod 6`.

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.Groups.zmod6_cosets >}}

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The proposition has a picture on the hexagon of @fig-coset-z6. Adding $1$ rotates the hexagon by $60^\circ$ and adding $2$
by $120^\circ$, and the two inscribed triangles respond differently to these rotations.

::: {#exm-cosq-z6-hexagon}
#### Parity on the hexagon

The cosets $\{0, 2, 4\}$ and $\{1, 3, 5\}$ are the two triangles inscribed in the hexagon. Adding an even residue rotates
by a multiple of $120^\circ$ and maps each triangle to itself, while adding an odd residue maps each triangle to the
other; the quotient $\mathbb{Z}_2$ records only which triangle a vertex lies on.
:::

The subgroup $\{0, 2, 4\}$ is not the only non-trivial subgroup of $\mathbb{Z}_6$. Slicing by the other one gives three
cosets instead of two and a quotient of order three.

::: {#exm-cosq-z6-thirds}
#### The cosets of $\{0, 3\}$

The cosets of $K = \{0, 3\}$ are $\{0, 3\}$, $\{1, 4\}$ and $\{2, 5\}$, the three pairs of opposite vertices of the
hexagon; the coset of a sum depends only on the residues modulo $3$ of the summands, and $\mathbb{Z}_6/K$ has the
addition table of $\mathbb{Z}_3$ (@exr-cosq-z6-addition-table).
:::

The parity rule of the proposition is inherited from the integers. The cosets of the even integers in $\mathbb{Z}$ obey
the same rule, and $\mathbb{Z}_6$ only remembers it.

::: {#exm-cosq-z-parity}
#### Even and odd integers

In $(\mathbb{Z}, +)$ the subgroup $2\mathbb{Z}$ has the two cosets of even and odd integers, and the quotient
$\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$ is $\mathbb{Z}_2$. Reducing modulo $6$ first and then taking parity gives the same answer
as taking parity directly, because $2$ divides $6$; this is why the cosets of @prp-z6-cosets are well defined.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The proposition can be checked by hand on $36$ pairs, or by a few lines of Sage. The first exercise prints the addition
tables of the cosets for both non-trivial subgroups of $\mathbb{Z}_6$.

::: {#exr-cosq-z6-addition-table}
#### Addition tables of cosets

For $H = \{0, 2, 4\}$ and for $K = \{0, 3\}$, list the cosets in $\mathbb{Z}_6$, check that the coset of $a + b$ depends
only on the cosets of $a$ and $b$, and compare the resulting tables with $\mathbb{Z}_2$ and $\mathbb{Z}_3$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Numbering the cosets by their smallest element, the coset of $a + b$ is the coset of $(a \bmod d) + (b \bmod d)$ with $d
= 2$ for $H$ and $d = 3$ for $K$, so the tables are addition modulo $2$ and modulo $3$:

{{< sage exr-cosq-z6-addition-table >}}
:::

Checking the thirty-six cases confirms the rule without explaining it; a short argument explains why all cases work. The second exercise asks for that
argument, which uses only that the subgroup is closed under subtraction.

::: {#exr-cosq-z6-by-hand}
#### The parity rule by hand

Show that if $a - a' \in H$ and $b - b' \in H$ for a subgroup $H$ of an abelian group, then $(a + b) - (a' + b') \in H$.
Deduce the second statement of @prp-z6-cosets without enumerating cases, and explain why the argument needs
commutativity (or normality).
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$(a + b) - (a' + b') = (a - a') + (b - b')$, which lies in $H$ as a sum of two elements of $H$. So $a + b$ and $a' + b'$
lie in the same coset whenever $a, a'$ and $b, b'$ do; for $H = \{0, 2, 4\}$ this is the parity rule. The rearrangement
$(a + b) - (a' + b') = (a - a') + (b - b')$ uses commutativity; in a non-abelian group the corresponding step is the
conjugation of @exr-cosq-well-defined, which needs $H$ normal.
:::

The two subgroups of $\mathbb{Z}_6$ are instances of a pattern valid for every cyclic group. The third exercise states
and proves it.

::: {#exr-cosq-zn-quotients}
#### Quotients of cyclic groups

For $d \mid n$, show that the cosets of $\langle d \rangle$ in $\mathbb{Z}_n$ are the $d$ residue classes modulo $d$ and
that their addition table is that of $\mathbb{Z}_d$. Check the count of cosets against Lagrange's theorem, and list
all quotients of $\mathbb{Z}_6$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\langle d \rangle = \{0, d, 2d, \dots\}$ consists of the residues divisible by $d$, and has $n/d$ elements. Two residues
lie in the same coset iff their difference is divisible by $d$, i.e. iff they agree modulo $d$ (this is consistent
because $d \mid n$). There are $d = n/(n/d)$ cosets, as Lagrange's theorem requires, and the class of a sum is the sum
of the classes modulo $d$. For $\mathbb{Z}_6$: $\mathbb{Z}_6/\langle 1 \rangle$ is trivial, $\mathbb{Z}_6/\langle 2
\rangle$ is $\mathbb{Z}_2$, $\mathbb{Z}_6/\langle 3 \rangle$ is $\mathbb{Z}_3$ and $\mathbb{Z}_6/\{0\}$ is $\mathbb{Z}_6$.
:::
::::

## Homomorphisms {#sec-homomorphisms}
