::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$D_4$ has the identity, five elements of order $2$ (the half turn and four reflections) and two of order $4$. Its ten
subgroups (@exr-grp-subgroups-d4) have orders dividing $8$, and six of them are normal: the trivial group, the centre,
the three subgroups of index $2$ and $D_4$. $D_4/Z$ is the Klein four-group (@exr-cosq-quotient-d4). The orbit of a vertex
has $4$ points and its stabiliser, the reflection in the diagonal through it, has order $2$: $4 \cdot 2 = 8$. There are
five conjugacy classes: $\{e\}$, $\{r^2\}$, the two quarter turns, the two diagonal reflections and the two edge
reflections. The diagonal reflections are transpositions of two vertices and the quarter turns four-cycles, both odd;
the kernel of the sign is $\{e, r^2\}$ together with the two edge reflections, a normal subgroup of index $2$. Finally
there are five irreducible representations of dimensions $1, 1, 1, 1, 2$ (@exr-repn-irreps-d4):

{{< sage exr-grpint-d4-full >}}
:::

The second integrative exercise turns an action on cosets into a homomorphism and identifies its kernel. It connects
cosets, actions, normal subgroups, kernels and the first isomorphism theorem.

::: {#exr-grpint-coset-action}
#### The homomorphism of an action on cosets

Let $G$ act on the left cosets $G/H$ by $g \cdot xH = gxH$, and let $\pi(g)$ be the permutation of $G/H$ induced by $g$.
(a) Show that $\pi$ is a homomorphism from $G$ to the group of permutations of $G/H$, with kernel $\bigcap_{x \in G}
xHx^{-1}$. (b) For $G = S_3$ and $H = \{e, (1\,2)\}$, show that the kernel is trivial and deduce from
@exr-cosq-action-perm that $\pi$ is an isomorphism onto the permutations of three cosets. (c) For $G = S_3$ and $H = A_3$,
find the kernel and the image, and compare with the sign. (d) What is the kernel of the action of $SO(3)$ on $SO(3)/SO(2) =
S^2$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
(a) $\pi(gh)$ sends $xH$ to $ghxH = \pi(g)(\pi(h)(xH))$, so $\pi(gh) = \pi(g) \circ \pi(h)$ by the action axioms
(@def-group-action). An element $g$ is in the kernel iff $gxH = xH$ for every $x$, i.e. iff $x^{-1}gx \in H$, i.e. iff $g
\in xHx^{-1}$, for every $x$; the kernel is a normal subgroup contained in $H$ (@def-kernel). (b) The conjugates of $H$
are the three subgroups $\{e, (i\,j)\}$ (@exm-normal-not), whose intersection is $\{e\}$; $\pi$ is injective, and since
$S_3$ and the permutations of three objects both have six elements, it is a bijection, an isomorphism (@def-isomorphism).
(c) $A_3$ is normal, so the kernel is $A_3$ itself; the image is the group of permutations of the two cosets, $\{\pm 1\}$,
and $\pi$ is the sign: $S_3/A_3 \cong \{\pm 1\}$ by @thm-first-isomorphism. (d) The kernel is the intersection of the
stabilisers of all points of the sphere, the rotations fixing every point, which is $\{e\}$; the action is faithful,
though not free (@exm-stabiliser-free).
:::

The third integrative exercise studies one representation from every point of view of the chapter. The cyclic
permutation of three coordinates is a homomorphism, an action with orbits and stabilisers, and a representation whose
commutant Schur's lemma predicts.

::: {#exr-grpint-cyclic-rep}
#### The cyclic group of order three on three coordinates

Let $\mathbb{Z}_3$ act on $\mathbb{C}^3$ by $k \mapsto C^k$, where $C$ sends $e_1 \to e_2 \to e_3 \to e_1$. (a) Show that $k
\mapsto C^k$ is an injective homomorphism into $GL(3, \mathbb{C})$. (b) Find the orbits and stabilisers of the action on the
set $\{e_1, e_2, e_3\}$ and check the orbit-stabiliser theorem. (c) Decompose the representation into the characters
$k \mapsto \omega^{jk}$ of @exm-rep-zn, using @exr-repn-invariant-z3. (d) Predict from Schur's lemma the dimension of the
space of matrices commuting with $C$, and show that these are exactly the matrices $a + bC + cC^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
(a) $C^3 = 1$, so $k \mapsto C^k$ is well defined on $\mathbb{Z}_3$ and $C^{j + k} = C^jC^k$; $C$ and $C^2$ are not the
identity, so the kernel is trivial. (b) The basis vectors form one orbit of $3$ points, each with trivial stabiliser:
$3 \cdot 1 = 3$, and the action is free and transitive. (c) The eigenvectors $(1, 1, 1)$, $(1, \bar\omega, \omega)$ and $(1,
\omega, \bar\omega)$ have eigenvalues $1, \omega, \bar\omega$, so the representation is the sum of the three characters
$j = 0, 1, 2$, each once; it is the regular representation of $\mathbb{Z}_3$. (d) Three inequivalent one-dimensional
summands give a commutant of dimension $3$ (@exr-repn-schur-s3): in the eigenbasis it consists of the diagonal matrices.
The matrices $1, C, C^2$ commute with $C$ and are linearly independent (their entries occupy disjoint positions), so they
span the commutant: it is the space of **circulant** matrices $a + bC + cC^2$.
:::
::::
